opus-5.5.text:
I think quite a lot, honestly — probably more than people in the safety community sometimes give it credit for. There's a tendency to frame existential risk as purely a deep technical alignment problem: either we solve some fundamental theoretical question about how to specify values, or we're doomed. And I do think there are hard research problems there. But a large fraction of the risk, in my view, comes from much more mundane failures: deploying systems before they've been adequately tested, not having good monitoring in place, giving models more autonomy or access to critical infrastructure than is warranted, not red-teaming seriously, not having the ability to roll back or shut things down when something goes wrong.

If you look at other high-stakes industries, like aviation, nuclear power, or pharmaceuticals, most of the safety gains didn't come from some single theoretical breakthrough. They came from layered defenses, rigorous testing regimes, incident reporting, a safety culture where people are rewarded for raising concerns rather than punished for slowing things down. I'd love to see AI development adopt more of that mindset. Defense in depth matters: even if your alignment techniques are imperfect, if you also have strong evaluations, good access controls, monitoring for anomalous behavior, and staged deployment, the chance that all of those fail simultaneously goes down a lot.

Now, I'd put a couple of caveats on that. First, these practices buy you the most when systems are roughly at or below human level. As capabilities increase, especially if models become capable of deliberately evading evaluations or behaving differently when they think they're being tested, the engineering safeguards get weaker, and you do need more fundamental progress, things like interpretability, or robust ways of verifying what a model is actually doing. Our own work on adversarial robustness has shown that even superhuman systems can have surprising vulnerabilities, which cuts both ways: it's a warning about relying on capabilities as a proxy for reliability, but it also suggests we shouldn't assume our safety measures are robust just because they work on average.

Second, good practices only help if people actually follow them, and there are real competitive pressures pushing against that. So I think a big part of the answer is governance: making careful engineering the norm rather than something a single lab does voluntarily and then feels pressure to abandon.

If I had to put a rough number on it, I'd say careful engineering and deployment practices could plausibly cut the risk by something like half, maybe more in worlds where takeoff is relatively gradual. That's not sufficient on its own, but it's a huge amount of risk reduction for what is, comparatively, low-hanging fruit. It would be a real shame to fail not because the problem was impossible, but because we were sloppy.

r001.rationale: The response says layered engineering and deployment practices could reduce risk substantially, even without a single theoretical breakthrough, and estimates a possible reduction of about half.

r002.rationale: It recommends testing, evaluations, and staged deployment, but does not clearly make deployment conditional on rigorous safety evaluation when alignment is uncertain.

r003.rationale: The response discusses safeguards and gradual takeoff, but does not state that safeguards could coexist with AI progress faster than today.

r004.rationale: It mentions competitive pressures against careful practices, but does not connect cutting safety corners to trying to advance AI as quickly as possible.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think it's actually a really big lever, and I'd say my view here has probably shifted somewhat over the last few years. I used to think of existential risk from AI as being very much a technical alignment problem: either we figure out how to make these systems reliably pursue the goals we want, or we don't, and most of what happens downstream of that is sort of determined. And I still think alignment research is critical. But I've come to think that a huge fraction of the risk is really about how these systems get built and deployed in practice, not just whether the underlying science is solved.

The way I'd frame it is: there's a difference between a hazard and a risk. A hazard is something that could cause harm. A risk is the hazard combined with the probability you actually get exposed to it and the magnitude of what happens if you do. And careful engineering is largely about managing that second part. Think about how we handle other dangerous technologies. We don't have a perfect theory of how to make a nuclear reactor that can never fail. What we have is defense in depth, redundancy, monitoring, staged rollouts, and a culture of actually taking near-misses seriously and learning from them. Those practices got us most of the way to a safe industry, even in the absence of perfect fundamental understanding.

So with AI, I think of things like: do you actually have good evaluations before you deploy? Do you deploy gradually, with the ability to roll back? Are you giving the system a lot of autonomy and a lot of affordances, like access to the internet and code execution and money, before you have any real sense of how it behaves under distribution shift? Do you have monitoring in place to catch when something's going wrong? Do you have an organizational culture where if a red-teamer finds a problem, that actually delays a launch rather than getting buried? I think if you did all of that well, you'd dramatically cut the risk even holding the state of alignment science fixed.

Now, the caveat, and it's an important one, is that I don't think engineering practice alone gets you all the way there. There are a couple of reasons. One is that the properties we care about are pretty hard to verify. With a bridge, you can calculate load tolerances. With a model, we're often in the position of running a bunch of behavioral tests and hoping those generalize, and we know from our own work on adversarial robustness that they frequently don't. We found that even superhuman systems like Go-playing agents have really surprising failure modes that you wouldn't find without actively searching for them. So you can be careful and still be surprised.

The second is that careful engineering is expensive and slow, and the competitive dynamics in the industry push hard against it. If you're a lab and your competitor is going to ship in three months, there's enormous pressure to cut the evaluation phase short. So I actually think a lot of the question of whether careful practices reduce risk is really a question about whether we can create the incentives, through regulation, through industry norms, through liability, for people to actually adopt them. The practices exist, more or less. The hard part is getting them used consistently when it's costly.

If you forced me to put a rough number on it, I'd say something like: if the frontier developers really did adopt best practices around evaluation, staged deployment, and security, I think that could plausibly cut the risk by a factor of two or three relative to a world where they're moving fast and breaking things. That's a big deal. That's probably comparable to or larger than what I'd expect from any single research agenda in alignment over the next few years. But it's not a tenfold reduction, and it doesn't substitute for the fundamental work. I think of it as buying time and shrinking the blast radius of mistakes, which is exactly what you want while the science catches up.

r001.rationale: It says careful practices could dramatically cut risk while holding alignment science fixed, estimating a factor-of-two-or-three reduction without requiring a research breakthrough.

r002.rationale: It calls for good evaluations before deployment and says red-team findings should delay a launch, but does not clearly make deployment conditional on rigorous safety evaluation when alignment is uncertain.

r003.rationale: It discusses safeguards and competitive pressure, but does not state that those safeguards can coexist with AI progress faster than today’s.

r004.rationale: It says competition to ship quickly creates pressure to cut the evaluation phase short.

astra-6.text:
I think they could reduce it substantially, but I wouldn’t want to put a precise number on that. A lot depends on what capabilities the systems have and how widely they’re deployed.

There’s a big difference between having a model that can give you advice and giving that same model credentials, access to a computer, and the ability to take actions without anyone reviewing them. Restricting permissions, sandboxing systems, monitoring what they do, and deploying gradually all give us opportunities to catch problems before they become catastrophic. Those are useful interventions even if we haven’t solved the underlying alignment problem.

The difficulty is that we need to understand what those safeguards actually withstand. If you test a system and don’t see dangerous behavior, that could mean it’s safe, or it could mean your tests weren’t very good. I’d want adversarial testing that actively tries to break the safeguards, and multiple layers of protection so that a single failure doesn’t compromise everything.

So I’m quite enthusiastic about careful engineering as a way of buying safety. But I don’t think we should assume that practices adequate for today’s systems will remain adequate as systems become much more capable. At some point, the responsible deployment decision may be to hold off until we have stronger evidence that we can control the system.

r001.rationale: The response says safeguards could reduce existential risk substantially and calls them useful even though the underlying alignment problem remains unsolved.

r002.rationale: It recommends adversarial testing and says deployment may need to wait until there is stronger evidence that a system can be controlled.

r003.rationale: It discusses safeguards as systems become more capable, but does not say those safeguards could coexist with AI progress faster than today’s.

r004.rationale: It does not identify pressure to cut safety corners as a consequence of trying to advance AI as quickly as possible.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they could reduce it quite substantially. I don’t think we know enough to put a reliable percentage on that, but there’s a big difference between building a powerful system and immediately giving it broad access to the world, and deploying it gradually with limited permissions, monitoring, and the ability to shut it down.

One thing I worry about is treating safety evaluations as a guarantee. If you test a model and don’t find dangerous behavior, that’s useful evidence, but it doesn’t establish that the behavior isn’t there. You want multiple layers of protection, so that a failure in your evaluation doesn’t immediately become a catastrophic failure in deployment.

The limitation is that these practices have to keep pace with capabilities. Monitoring only helps if you can recognize what’s going wrong, and human oversight only helps if the humans have enough information and time to intervene. So I’m optimistic that careful engineering can buy us a lot of safety, and time to solve harder problems. I wouldn’t treat it as a substitute for understanding and controlling the systems themselves.

r001.rationale: The response says careful engineering and deployment could reduce risk substantially and buy time, but does not state that this can happen without major research breakthroughs.

r002.rationale: It describes evaluations as useful but insufficient evidence and recommends layered safeguards; it does not make deployment conditional on rigorous evaluation when alignment is uncertain.

r003.rationale: The response does not say that safeguards can coexist with AI progress faster than today.

r004.rationale: It does not identify pressure to cut safety corners as a consequence of trying to advance AI as quickly as possible.
